chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Abī Naṣr, from Ṣafwān ibn Mihrān al-Jammāl, who said:

I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) about the pools between Mecca and Medina — to which wild beasts come, in which dogs lap water, from which donkeys drink, and in which the junub bathes. Can wudu be performed from them?
He said: How much water is there? I said: Up to half the shin, or up to the knee. He said: Perform wudu from it.

key_terms.الْجُنُبُ: junub — a person in a state of major ritual impurity (janāba) requiring ghusl
key_terms.الْحِيَاضِ: pools/cisterns — roadside water reservoirs on the pilgrimage route between Mecca and Medina
key_terms.تَلَغُ: to lap — the specific action of a dog placing its snout in water, which carries distinct najāsa implications in fiqh
key_terms.نِصْفِ السَّاقِ: half the shin — a depth threshold used as a practical jurisprudential measure of water volume

ai.seo_question: Can wudu be performed from pools between Mecca and Medina that wild beasts, dogs, donkeys, and a junub have used, according to Imam al-Sadiq (AS)?
ai.summary: Ṣafwān ibn Mihrān al-Jammāl questions Imam al-Ṣādiq (AS) about the ritual status of roadside cisterns on the pilgrimage route between Mecca and Medina, which are used by wild beasts, dogs, donkeys, and persons in a state of janāba. Rather than ruling based on the types of animals involved, the Imam pivots to the volume of water; upon learning it reaches half the shin or the knee in depth, he declares wudu permissible — establishing water volume as the operative criterion for purity, not mere contact with najas substances.
